title: Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan Apologize for Laughing at “Insensitive Joke” About Charlie Kirk on ‘I’ve Had It’ Podcast
full_text: × Skip to main content By McKinley Franklin Plus Icon McKinley Franklin View All November 7, 2026 7:08pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Jennifer Welch and Angie Sullivan Theo Wargo/Getty Images I’ve Had It podcast hosts Jennifer Welch and Angie “Pumps” Sullivan have released an apology statement for laughing at a joke about Charlie Kirk on the Thursday episode of their show. “On Thursday’s show, we laughed at a joke about Charlie Kirk. It was an insensitive joke, and we should not have laughed. We regret it, and we apologize,” they wrote in a statement shared on the I’ve Had It podcast Instagram Saturday. “Whatever our political differences, there is nothing funny about gun violence. We’ve long supported common-sense gun safety reform. To that end, we’ve made a donation to Everytown for Gun Safety, the largest gun violence prevention organization in America.” Related Stories TV Pete Davidson Makes Shocking Charlie Kirk Joke at Kevin Hart Roast News The Widow and the Firebrand: How Candace Owens Turned a Conservative Succession Into a Crusade Against Erika Kirk During the Thursday episode of the podcast, the hosts read posts made by online users amid the 2026 midterm results. They read one that said, “We’re digging up Charlie Kirk and doing it again,” and they both laughed. (That segment of the Thursday episode has since been cut out, but was reshared online.) “We’ll keep using our platforms to fight for the safety of all Americans,” Welch and Sullivan’s joint statement concluded. Kirk died in September 2025 after being fatally shot while speaking at a college event in Utah County, Utah. On Thursday, in response to a video of the cut clip from I’ve Had It on X , Cash App announced they were no longer sponsors of the podcast. “We do not condone violence of any kind, and we are no longer sponsors of this podcast,” Cash App wrote. Boll & Branch, a luxury bedding company, also said they would not “advertise with the I’ve Had It podcast and will not in the future.” Chewy additionally put out a statement noting they “do not sponsor or support the I’ve Had It podcast. We unequivocally condemn violence in all forms. The comments made by the hosts do not reflect Chewy’s values or what we stand for as a company.” Nov. 7, 7:45 p.m. Updated to include Chewy’s statement. THR

title: Taiwan’s Mirror Fiction Hands Out $50,000 In Awards For Book To Screen Adaptations
full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Taiwan’s Mirror Fiction Hands Out $50,000 In Awards For Book To Screen Adaptations Taiwan’s Chunghwa Telecom Unveils Investment Slate Headed By ‘Gunshot’ & ‘Call Of Lobster’ Toei CEO Fumio Yoshimura Talks Global Expansion, GenAI Adoption & Entry Into Games View All November 7, 2026 5:11pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source 5th Edition of Mirror Fiction Awards TAICCA Mirror Fiction , a Taiwanese IP development and production outfit, handed out cash prizes worth more than $50,000 to two authors, to help them publish their works and adapt them for screen, in the fifth edition of its biennial awards. The announcement was made at Taiwan Creative Content Fest ( TCCF ), where Mirror Fiction also unveiled its latest line-up of IPs. Iris Kong was presented with the Grand Prize of $30,500 (NTD1M) for The Stand-In Family , a work about a group of people who are not related but are living together as a family so they can secure ownership of a house. Related Stories News Taiwan's Chunghwa Telecom Unveils Investment Slate Headed By 'Gunshot' & 'Call Of Lobster' News Toei CEO Fumio Yoshimura Talks Global Expansion, GenAI Adoption & Entry Into Games An engineer by profession, Kong said she kept the potential for film and TV adaptation in mind during the writing process, while also striving to ensure the narrative remained compelling and thought-provoking for readers. “I look forward to the story being published and, perhaps, reaching an even wider audience on screen,” said Kong. Watch on Deadline Malaysian author Liang Xuan won the $21,000 (NTD700,000) Jury Prize for Endless Rain , set in a predominantly ethnic Chinese town in Ipoh, Malaysia, drawing from the experiences of her mother and grandfather’s generations. The story follows a mysterious woman who appears in town more than 20 years after she was supposedly murdered. Both works will be developed for publication and potential film or television adaptation by Mirror Fiction. Previous winners of the awards include Port Of Lies , which won the Grand Prize at the second edition and became an award-winning TV series. The awards are supported by property developer Sinyi Realty. Speaking at the awards ceremony, Mirror Fiction General Manager Tung Cheng-yu noted that films adapted from books outperform those based on original screenplays at the box office by an average of over 40%. Viewership for TV series adapted from books is nearly 60% higher. Book editor Patrick Chia, representing the jury for the awards, said the quality of this year’s finalists was consistently high and there was a significant increase in science fiction and fantasy entries, in particular stories set in a dystopian near future or dealing with the impact of new technologies. Lu Yiwen, who won the Grand Prize in the fourth edition of the competition, shared her experience of working with Mirror Fiction after winning the award, which in addition to financial support involves mentorship from experienced editors. “Writing has evolved from something I did in my daily life into a serious endeavor – and, ultimately, my career. I’m grateful for this award, which has truly solidified my identity as a creator,” Lu said. Mirror Fiction also unveiled a slate of new novels suitable for adaptation at the event, including Kevin Chen’s 036037 , about two middle-aged individuals finding closure in their relationship after two decades; Tommy Tan’s crime thriller The Midnight Masseur , in which the art of massage becomes a form of intelligence-gathering; and Hsieh Shu-yu’s Diplomatic Brother s, about two brothers – a diplomat and a strategist for an organized crime syndicate – who swap identities. Chen’s novel Ghost Town has been translated into 13 languages, including English. title: Camerimage Opens With Minute Of Silence For Kraków Mass Shooting; Darren Aronofsky Honored & Luca Guadagnino Introduces ‘Artificial’
full_text: Skip to main content By Diana Lodderhose Diana Lodderhose International Features Editor @dianalodderhose More Stories By Diana Camerimage Opens With Minute Of Silence For Kraków Mass Shooting; Darren Aronofsky Honored & Luca Guadagnino Introduces ‘Artificial’ International Disruptors: Studio N Chief Mikyung Kwon On The Value Of Webcomic IP & Taking Risks With Korean Epic ‘The Remarried Empress’ Antonin Baudry & Simon Abkarian Talk French Box Office Hit ‘De Gaulle’: “The National Icon Did Not Exist In 1940” View All November 7, 2026 4:37pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Darren Aronofsky at Camerimage in 2026. Deadline There was a sombre mood at the opening ceremony of this year’s Camerimage Film Festival as organizers kicked off its 34th edition in Toruń, Poland with a minute’s silence for the victims of the mass shooting in Kraków, which happened a few hours before the event began. According to reports, at least six people are now dead, and more than a dozen injured when a gunman, who is suspected to have ties to far-right ideologies, drove into Kraków’s historic Main Market Square and opened fire. Poland’s Prime Minister Donald Tusk said three bodies were also later found at the suspect’s home. It is the country’s deadliest shooting in decades. Related Stories News Andrew Garfield Does Not Recall Waving At Sam Altman On 'Artificial' Set: "Very Confused By That" News Camerimage: Hype Williams & Darren Aronofsky Set For Honorary Awards Local politicians scheduled to speak at the Camerimage opening proceedings acknowledged the severity of the shooting, which has sent shockwaves across the country today, before opening ceremony proceedings began. Watch on Deadline The festival kicked off Saturday night (November 7) at Toruń’s Jordanski Culture Centre. AI was a major theme during the three-hour ceremony with festival director Marek Zydowicz bringing a humanoid robot to the stage which engaged with him as he stressed that the “hopes and threats” of AI would be a major talking point throughout the 7-day event. The ceremony was frequently interspersed with footage of Francis Ford Coppola, Gal Gadot, Christopher Nolan, Maggie Gyllenhaal, Steven Spielberg and Ben Affleck who all weighed in on the subject of AI in the entertainment space. Aronofsky, who has been a big proponent of using generative AI in filmmaking after launching his creative studio Primordial Soup last year, was honored with Camerimage’s honorary Award for Director. The Requiem for a Dream and Black Swan helmer said it was his third time at Camerimage, and he hoped to keep returning to the Polish event. “The reason I come back is because there’s very rarely film festivals that celebrate the collaboration of everyone,” he said. “They’re very focused on not just the flashy names and that’s really incredible because it honors everyone who makes films possible for people like me.” Karolina Gruszka, one of Poland’s most acclaimed film and theatre actresses, was honored with the Marshal of the Kujawy Pomorze Region Film Award this year. The prolific actress also starred in David Lynch’s last film Inland Empire, and she gave a nod to the late director calling him a “master investigator” of stories. Polish cinematographer and longtime Steven Spielberg collaborator Janusz Kamiński received an award from Deadline’s sister publication THR while Camerimage also paid tribute to Andrzej Wajda, the legendary Polish director behind titles such as The Promised Land and Ashes and Diamonds . This year marks a century since Wajda’s birth and a decade since his death, with Poland’s Senate declaring this year ‘The Year of Wajda’ in the country. Humanoid robot at Camerimage 2026. The opening film this evening at Camerimage was Luca Guadagnino ’s OpenAI origin story Artificial , starring Andrew Garfield as Sam Altman and Yura Borisov as key creative Ilya Sutskever. The director was joined on stage with the film’s cinematographer Malik Hassan Sayeed where the pair discussed the creative process of the film, which is set to be released by Neon in the U.S. on December 25 and in the UK on January 22, 2027. “I’ve been interested and kind of curious about the personalities of what they call tech oligarchs or tech bros for a while,” Guadagnino said. “And when I got the script that Simon Rich wrote, the world he was describing was an immediate hook for me because there was a lot in that that could be told about the dynamics of power and narcissism but at the same time it was an unprecedented setup for showing how very few people control societies.” When pressed about whether there were constraints from a legal perspective when making a film featuring real people like Altman and Sutskever, Guadagnino said: “The only constraints we gave ourselves were facts. We wanted it to be factual, and we didn’t want to dramatize anything.” He continued: “I’m very proud because, of course, you don’t make movies for vetting it through legal, but the very interesting thing is that this movie is 100% vetted by the legal business [and] sometimes the reality is more surprising than fantasy.” Camerimage takes place November 7-14, 2026. ‘Heated Rivalry’ Hat Trick: Hit Series Filming Season 2, Season 3 And A Movie Cameos By James Talarico, Emma Stone; Druski In Whiteface As Elizabeth Holmes ‘Godzilla’ Stalks $32M U.S. Bow, Best For Live-Action Foreign-Language Pic LACMA 2026 Art+Film Gala Red Carpet: Andrew Garfield, Anya Taylor-Joy & More Read More About: Comments

title: Emmy Rossum On RAINN Ambassadorship, “Continuing The Conversation” About Sexual Violence After ‘Furious’ Role
full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn Emma Stone Joins Druski For His ‘SNL’ Debut Opening Monologue While Filming ‘The Catch’ Rom-Com Emmy Rossum On RAINN Ambassadorship, “Continuing The Conversation” About Sexual Violence After ‘Furious’ Role Christopher Nolan On DGA “Holding The Studios To Account” In Protecting Copyright From AI, Including Anti-AI Boilerplate In ‘The Odyssey’ View All November 7, 2026 4:22pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Emmy Rossum in 'Furious' Sarah Shatz/Hulu/Disney/Courtesy Everett Collection As Emmy Rossum prepares to return for Season 2 of Furious , she’s keeping the show’s themes close to heart. The Golden Globe nominee, who recently joined RAINN ‘s anti-sexual violence organization as an ambassador, explained that she wants to “take the shame out of the conversation” after playing FBI agent Alice Black, who has to track down a survivor of trafficking. “I think it’s so important to continue the conversation, especially now, because sexual violence is a real problem,” she told the Associated Press . “It’s prevalent for so many women, and it will be in the room tonight, statistically. So, it’s something we must take the shame out of the conversation around it, and learn how to talk about it. I feel, growing up, that sexual violence was not something I knew how to talk about, certainly not something I would feel comfortable talking about with my family.” Related Stories News Emmy Rossum & ‘Furious’ Creator Liz Meriwether On Interviewing Real Trafficking Survivors, Updating A 1987 Thriller & Season 2 “Croatian Beach” Dreams Cancellations and Renewals ‘Furious’ Renewed For Season 2 By Hulu Ahead Of Season 1 Finale Rossum added, “So, being able to partner with an organization that is helping survivors with longterm trauma, with immediate trauma, and also just helping educate us how to not just be part of the solution, but part of prevention as well. I’m talking to much younger kids about consent, and I’m seeing that start even for my daughter, who’s 5, being able to say, ‘please don’t touch my hair’ when she doesn’t want that. So, that kind of empowering language for young people, I think is incredibly important. So, educating myself and others is something I’m very passionate about.” Watch on Deadline Rossum previously told Deadline that she spoke with real survivors of sexual violence and trafficking in researching for her Furious role, noting it was “very important for us to really show women in all of their complexity,” citing her complex character Alice. Emmy Rossum wants to use her crime drama "Furious" to "take the shame out of the conversation" around sexual violence. She spoke at the Women in Film Honors. #EmmyRossum #Furious pic.twitter.com/0vc6QCdG5n — The Associated Press (@AP) November 7, 2026 “It’s these kinds of contradictions that don’t immediately make sense and that don’t add up to a perfect victim, in the way that our justice system likes them to be, in order to be quote unquote ‘deserving of justice,’ or in order for their story to make sense,” she said. “Trauma doesn’t make sense. Violence doesn’t make sense. The aftereffects that it leaves in you don’t make sense. title: Camerimage Founder Marek Zydowicz on AI, Aronofsky and Why “Cinematographers Are Artists, Not Technicians”
full_text: × Skip to main content By Scott Roxborough Plus Icon Scott Roxborough Europe Bureau Chief sroxborough Follow Sign Up View All November 7, 2026 4:11pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Marek Żydowicz Camerimage Camerimage , the world’s premier festival devoted to the art of cinematography, turns 34 this year, and it arrives in Torun, Poland, Nov. 7-14, with its founder in both a combative and reflective mood. Marek Zydowicz, who launched the event in 1993 to champion cinematographers and other below-the-line artists the industry treated as mere technicians, is fielding questions on a thorny set of issues. Among them: the rise of generative AI , which gets its own debates and workshops this year; the squeeze on budgets and theatrical releases; and the decision to honor Darren Aronofsky , an outspoken AI adopter, with the festival’s director award. Related Stories Movies PÖFF Stands With Ukraine: A Look at Films Featured at Tallinn Made Despite, and Because of, the War Oscars 2027: Int'l Films in Focus 'Hold Onto Me,' Cyprus' First Oscar Hopeful, Stars a Newcomer and a 'Dogtooth' Actor in a Very Personal Father-Daughter Drama Joe Walker, the editor behind Dune and 12 Years a Slave , is also being feted and will chair the Main Competition jury, while Polish cinematographer Janusz Kaminski, whose Disclosure Day is screening in contention, receives THR ’s Visionary award . Speaking to THR ahead of this year’s fest, Zydowicz said Camerimage will remain open to a “diversity of techniques and technologies” but draws the line at fully AI-generated films. In a wide-ranging conversation, Zydowicz spoke about the festival’s growing ambitions, the reason why Poland seems to produce so many great cinematographers, and why the human eye will never be replaced. Why are there so many extraordinary Polish cinematographers? What’s the secret? A full answer would require going quite far back into the history of Polish cinema, and even further, to the period when Poland was partitioned. For 123 years, paintings and graphic works depicting the most important events in our nation’s history sustained our hopes of regaining independence and stirred our imaginations and dreams. After the second World War, this tradition of depicting the past played an enormously important role in laying the foundations of the Lodz Film School. Artists working under communist censorship often drew on the same ways of expressing what could not be said openly as their predecessors had in the nineteenth century. Sometimes the dialogue between characters told one story while the images suggested another. This encouraged the development of an extraordinary sensitivity and a search for ways of using composition to smuggle forbidden content and aesthetics into films. Technological limitations and Poland’s isolation from the most progressive developments in Western culture made it necessary to find original solutions of our own. During those difficult times, Polish filmmakers absorbed different cinematic traditions, both those that reached us legally and those that were banned and smuggled in from Western Europe and America. The relationship between the director and the cinematographer became an important factor in the creation of original forms of cinematic imagery. Many outstanding filmmakers taught in Lodz, and later at other Polish film schools as well. The film school taught the history of painting, and not only Polish painting. Over successive generations, an exceptionally strong artistic tradition emerged from this. That is what we see today in the diversity of Polish cinematographers’ work: from Hollywood productions to independent and art cinema around the world. Why did you choose Darren Aronofsky for your director honor this year? Do you expect a debate around his embrace of AI in production , which is still a very controversial subject in the industry? I do expect that discussion, because AI is an important and contentious subject, and Darren has shown that he wants to explore it professionally. Our award recognizes over thirty years of his filmmaking. His body of work provokes, unsettles and asks us to confront aspects of human nature from which we might prefer to look away. His films can be difficult to watch, but it is often precisely that discomfort that makes us look more closely at ourselves and others. His artistic achievements deserve awards. Think of the intensity with which Requiem for a Dream conveys the experience of addiction, or the way Black Swan draws us into its protagonist’s increasingly disturbed perception of reality. The Fountain explores love, mortality and spiritual longing through an extraordinarily ambitious visual imagination. It is a film I admire enormously, also for the risks it took and the resistance it encountered. The Whale , made on an entirely different scale, finds another way to bring us close to suffering and the desire for human connection. Darren Aronofsky Courtesy of Camerimage Darren moves between intimacy and spectacle, tenderness and brutality, sometimes bringing religious imagery into stories about deeply personal struggles. His films encourage audiences to question their own values and to notice people whose pain might otherwise go unseen. This combination of formal boldness and concern for human beings is one of the most important reasons we are honouring him. His interest in AI is a separate discussion, although it also reflects his continuing curiosity about the tools available to filmmakers. We are not presenting this award as a judgement on how he uses the technology. I do, however, appreciate his willingness, as an established artist, to explore unfamiliar territory. That curiosity has been evident throughout his career. We should discuss his experiments openly, including the disagreements they provoke. What is Camerimage’s policy towards AI — would you accept AI-generated work in your selection? We do not accept productions generated entirely by AI. Our selection focuses on the art of cinematographers. Of course, to understand AI as a tool for creating moving images, we watch films made entirely with AI. Personally, I am in favour of hybrid films in which the live actors appearing in them decide for themselves how far AI may intervene in the images being created. Within cinematography, we are open to a diversity of techniques and technologies, but always with respect for artists’ personal rights. A film may use extensive visual effects and digital post-production, or it may be made with very limited resources and rely almost entirely on techniques achieved on set, but it should always respect the wishes of the people lending their likenesses and voices. We value the cinematographer’s creative contribution to telling a story through film. Advanced digital techniques have long been part of that process. AI will, in time, find its proper place in this process. Everyone will use it. The only question is how. For now, curiosity about the future does not change our principles for selecting films for the festival competitions. The subject remains open, and we want to discuss it with a view to bringing about legal regulations, for example at European Union level, that will make AI safe for our industry. Explain the reasoning behind your other honoree, Joe Walker. Joe Walker is an outstanding editor whose work we have admired and presented for many years. His collaborations with Denis Villeneuve, including Sicario , Arrival , Blade Runner 2049 and the Dune films, demonstrate the expressive possibilities of editing on very different scales. He has helped give these films their distinctive rhythms and their ability to make an audience understand something before it is explained in words. In Arrival , the organization of time is fundamental to the way we experience the story. In Dune , the editing helps maintain the connection between a vast, complex world and the characters moving through it. Zendaya in Dune: Part Three. Courtesy of Everett His work with Steve McQueen, from Hunger to 12 Years a Slave and Widows , reveals an equally extraordinary sensitivity to performance, the duration of shots and silence. We are interested in how his editing gives images the power to affect us and shape the relationship between what we see and what we feel. This makes his contribution particularly relevant to a festival devoted to visual storytelling. We are delighted to honour him in Torun and give audiences the opportunity to speak with him about his films after their screenings. He has also agreed to chair the Main Competition jury. The eye of an editor with his experience and sensitivity brings a valuable perspective to a competition that means so much to us. THR is honoring Poland’s own Janusz Kaminski with its Visionary award this year . How would you sum up his contribution to the art of cinematography? We could easily devote the rest of this interview to Janusz’s contribution and still leave a great deal unsaid. He is one of the greatest cinematographers in the history of cinema. He created images that have become part of our shared cinematic memory in Schindler’s List and Saving Private Ryan . I am very interested in his search for the right form for the story contained in a screenplay. He chooses an approach to imagery that will fully convey its emotional truth. THR Visionary Award Winner Janusz Kaminski Gabriel Olsen/FilmMagic/Getty Images Our festival recognized The Diving Bell and the Butterfly , for which Janusz received the Golden Frog. It is a beautiful, painful and deeply moving film, with an extraordinary ability to bring us into another person’s experience. The cinematography is inseparable from that achievement. It reminds us that we should appreciate Janusz’s work beyond his collaboration with that brilliant and iconic master of cinema, Steven Spielberg. This year, I invited another of their films, Disclosure Day , to the Main Competition. Janusz’s unsettling cinematography, with frequent halation creating a sense of the presence of something unknown and alien, is crucial to the film as a whole. Janusz is a “visionary”, and his images have a profound effect on audiences and young filmmakers. Camerimage has traditionally championed the cinematographer as an artist in their own right, rather than simply a technical collaborator. Do you think the industry is doing enough to recognize the creative contribution of cinematographers, particularly during awards season? I would say both yes and no. Cinematography awards are presented in several places around the world. At the same time, most mainstream media coverage of films names only directors and actors, leaving out the cinematographers. The term “below the line” has an established meaning in the organization of a production, but it says very little about the artistic role of the people it describes. A cinematographer helps determine how we experience a film’s story and how closely we connect with its characters. They create the atmosphere of every frame on screen and the emotions and feelings of the characters. They are an artist, not a technician operating a camera. Our role is to help people understand and appreciate the artistry involved in this work, and to ensure that these artists have appropriate working conditions. Awards season is one opportunity to do this, but the conversation should continue throughout the year. What are the biggest challenges you see facing cinematographers and other below-the-line artists at the moment? Financial pressure is certainly one, particularly when filmmakers are expected to do more with fewer resources. There is also considerable anxiety about AI and what it may mean for people’s livelihoods. I understand those concerns, although I do not believe that an artist’s contribution can simply be replaced by a generated image. A cinematographer brings a lifetime of observations, relationships, emotions and experiences of the world to their work. All of this can inform a decision made on set in a fraction of a second. It has a decisive influence on the power of the moving image being created. Technology will change working methods, but I am certain that the human perspective which gives films a spiritual dimension remains indispensable. Younger filmmakers face a particular kind of pressure because they have grown up amid an almost constant influx of images and information. They are also entering a world in which it will become increasingly difficult to judge how an image was made and whether it records something that actually happened. I am cautious about generational labels, but these conditions are worth recognizing. My generation grew up with different constraints, so I would not pretend that our experiences are the same. Every generation has to understand its own circumstances and find a way to navigate them. There are also encouraging changes, including the growing participation of women in film productions dominated by men for decades. Jolanta Dylewska, who won our Golden Frog in 2011 and returns to the Main Competition this year [as the cinematographer of Through the Wall ], is one of the artists who helped break down those barriers. It is wonderful to see so many women creating outstanding work today. How would you describe the identity of Camerimage in 2026? Our identity remains rooted in the idea I set out at the first edition of the festival in 1993: Let us recognize excluded and marginalised artists, the cinematographers whom the industry largely treats as technicians. We want audiences to discover what images contribute to their experience of film. TorunCamerimage is a spiritual spa for film artists, who can talk here, free from pressure, about the language of the moving image and its significance in the contemporary world and in the future. There are occasional incidents and attempts to exert aggressive pressure on us as organisers, and on me as the founder and director of TorunCamerimage, but never between our guests. We will remain independent, respecting artistic and humanistic values. How has it changed over more than 30 years of operation, and what do you want the festival to become in the future? The most obvious change is the scale. We began in Torun, with a venue that was not a professional cinema. We searched for a suitable location in Poland and returned to Torun, whose authorities decided, together with the Polish government, to build the European Film Center Camerimage at a cost of around $200 million. The festival has grown, with an average annual attendance of around 70,000 across its events. Around 1,000 film school students and some 800 cinematographers from around the world attend, along with several hundred other creative professionals from our industry. In recent years, we have welcomed guests from more than 80 countries. Alongside the film studio, the European Film Center Camerimage will have an education centre, an exhibition and trade fair centre of around 4,000 square metres dedicated to presenting filmmaking techniques and technologies, and a large screening auditorium with more than 1,600 seats, capable of accommodating a wide variety of projection technologies. The complex will be completed by the House of Cinema, with several cinemas, including an IMAX-type auditorium, and the David Lynch’s World of Imagination. David gave me more than a dozen shipping containers of artefacts from Twin Peaks . I am working on the exhibition design that I agreed with David and that we intended to realise together. What advice do you have for a first-time Camerimage attendee? Come with a plan, but leave room to change it. Choose the films and events you particularly want to attend, remembering that schedules will overlap and some screenings may be full. An unexpected alternative may turn out to be the most valuable experience of your entire visit. We have seen this many times. Be active. Talk to the artists and other audience members. Take part in the Q&As after screenings and in workshops at Camerimage Film Studio. The festival continues beyond the screening room, as people share impressions, disagree, get to know one another and sometimes find the beginnings of a future collaboration. A little spontaneity and courage can take you a long way at TorunCamerimage. THR

title: Taiwan’s Chunghwa Telecom Unveils Investment Slate Headed By ‘Gunshot’ & ‘Call Of Lobster’
full_text: Skip to main content By Liz Shackleton Liz Shackleton pmc-media-editor-2024 More Stories By Liz Taiwan’s Mirror Fiction Hands Out $50,000 In Awards For Book To Screen Adaptations Taiwan’s Chunghwa Telecom Unveils Investment Slate Headed By ‘Gunshot’ & ‘Call Of Lobster’ Toei CEO Fumio Yoshimura Talks Global Expansion, GenAI Adoption & Entry Into Games View All November 7, 2026 4:00pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Gunshot PTS Taigi TV, S11 Partners, Third Culture Content Taiwanese telco Chunghwa Telecom announced a slate of film and series investments at Taiwan Creative Content Fest ( TCCF ), including police crime drama Gunshot , starring Kent Tsai, and Call Of Lobster , starring Choi Siwon and Chang Chen. Chunghwa is one of three Taiwanese telcos that are investing in film and TV content through funds launched in partnership with the Taiwanese government. The company’s previous content investments include feature films Arrested Memory , a Japan-Taiwan co-production directed by Sabu, and The Photo From 1977, directed by Frank Cheng and Sheng-Jung Tang. The two films have a combined 12 nominations in the upcoming Golden Horse Awards. The eight-part series is produced by PTS Taigi TV with S11 Partners and Third Culture Content . Chang Chen and Super Junior member Choi Siwon are set to star in the film, directed by Yin Chen-hao and produced by Calendar Studios . Chunghwa boarded the project after it won the Chunghwa Telecom Award at TCCF in 2024. Taiwan’s Ministry of Culture is also backing the film. Among other film investments, Chunghwa also announced its participation in Studio76’s Demon Of The East – Black Condo , part of a horror cinematic universe spanning four Asian countries. Outside of films and series, Chunghwa is also backing reality cooking show Next Z Chef and indie band Shallow Levée’s Speak in Silence Asian tour. title: Christopher Nolan On DGA “Holding The Studios To Account” In Protecting Copyright From AI, Including Anti-AI Boilerplate In ‘The Odyssey’
full_text: Skip to main content By Glenn Garner Glenn Garner Associate Editor @xoxo_glenn More Stories By Glenn Emma Stone Joins Druski For His ‘SNL’ Debut Opening Monologue While Filming ‘The Catch’ Rom-Com Emmy Rossum On RAINN Ambassadorship, “Continuing The Conversation” About Sexual Violence After ‘Furious’ Role Christopher Nolan On DGA “Holding The Studios To Account” In Protecting Copyright From AI, Including Anti-AI Boilerplate In ‘The Odyssey’ View All November 7, 2026 3:40pm Add us as a Google Preferred Source Christopher Nolan attends the 76th DGA Awards on Feb. 10, 2024 in Beverly Hills, California. Michael Buckner/PMC Halfway into his first time as DGA president, Christopher Nolan is holding the studios’ feet to the fire in protecting copyrighted materials from AI . In a new interview, the 2x Oscar winner explained that it’s “down to the studios” to go after AI recreations of their work, noting that he was “very pleased” his current Academy Award contender The Odyssey contains a legal warning against using the film to train AI data. “AI is too big a catchall term. It’s describing too many things and it’s being used by companies to absolve themselves of responsibility,” he explained on the Hollywood Insiders podcast. “They sort of want to portray it as this Frankenstein’s monster that can get out of control and can change the world without them having any accountability for it. We have to strongly resist that.” Related Stories News Christopher Nolan Says Directors Union Unlikely To Accept 5-Year Deal With AMPTP; DGA President Talks AI, Healthcare, Tax Incentives & More Ahead Of 2026 Bargaining News Christopher Nolan Elected DGA President, Ron Howard Among New Officers Nolan added, “There’s already legislation in place that protects people, protects creators, etc. And the fact that they these companies hide behind fair-use provisions, for example, I think longer term that won’t hold up in court. There have already been some significant judgments against it. We’re very focused at the Guild about holding the studios to account for protecting their copyrights. We can’t do that. With very few exceptions in the Guild, we are not the copyright holders of the films that we’ve worked on. It’s down to the studios to do that. Watch on Deadline “And I was very pleased to see that the boilerplate at the end of The Odyssey , for the first time, it contains a message saying that this film cannot be ingested and used as training data,” he said. Following his election as DGA president last September, after serving on the Guild’s Artificial Intelligence Committee, Nolan told Deadline there are “excellent protections” in place against AI, “ but that’s not enough .” “You have to have a voice in how this tool is used moving forward. Also, we like to try and have a voice in, what’s the legal framework?” explained Nolan. “Because we generally aren’t the copyright holders of our work, but our income, our residuals, depends on the appropriate monetization of those copyrights. So we’re constantly in dialogue with the companies about, are you maximizing the value of the work that we’ve created?
